model:deepseek|ver:4.1|title:zero mismat.content_excerpt: Last month, we showed that rollout and training can agree exactly. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, vLLM and the trainer produced the same logprob for every sampled token, bit for bit, on the fast kernels, with an 8.7% reduction in rollout throughput. An agent skill now does the alignment for each new model. That post was about synchronous RL, which has no weight lag, so zero mismatch removes the only gap between rollout and training. This post is about asynchronous RL, which is faster but off-policy by design. Does zero mismatch still matter there? We answer with a new paper from NVIDIA Research and Inferact (Jian Hu et al.): REINFORCE Zero: Kernel Alignment Unlocks Stable Asynchronous RL with Importance Sampling . All numbers in sections 2 to 4 come from it. In synchronous RL, rollout and training take turns, and each waits for the other. Asynchronous RL runs them at the same time: rollout keeps generating while the learner updates. The price is weight lag . A sample generated with weights version v is trained at version k > v. The gap k − v is not small: REINFORCE Zero runs at lag 2 and 8 on math reasoning, and at lag 64 on agentic tool use. So the learner always trains on samples from an older policy. The standard correction is importance sampling (IS): reweight each token by π / μ, the learner's probability for it divided by the probability the rollout recorded when it sampled it. The question is whether that correction covers the whole gap. π is the learner's computation and μ is the rollout engine's. The second term compares the two at the same weights θv. Weight lag changes smoothly. It telescopes over the most recent updates, and when each update is small it follows a smoothly changing policy trajectory. This is the gap IS is meant to correct. Kernel mismatch fluctuates. It depends on batch composition and numerical execution, so it introduces fluctuations even when rollout and learner use identical weights. Figure 1: Peak-to-median ratio of the importance-weight deviation D3, log scale, for two asynchronous runs on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: REINFORCE Zero with aligned kernels and IS with standard kernels. Source: REINFORCE Zero, Table 2. The REINFORCE Zero paper measures this with D3, the per-update average of w − 1 − log w over tokens, where w is the importance weight. model:vllm|title:introducing kinference.content_excerpt: We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference] , a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks , we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type. By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our unloaded latency benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our capacity benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn . model:vllm|title:migrating vllm to the l.content_excerpt: vLLM relies heavily on PyTorch, with frequent calls to LibTorch in its C++ backend. As a result, changes to LibTorch’s binary interface may require vLLM to be rebuilt and relinked, even when the APIs remain unchanged. What if we could update LibTorch without rebuilding vLLM? That’s where the LibTorch Stable ABI comes in. With a LibTorch Stable ABI, updating LibTorch does not require rebuilding or updating vLLM in order to keep using it. Instead, we could swap out the torch wheel and import it directly into our vLLM package. As of v0.33.0, vLLM publishes LibTorch ABI Stable CUDA wheels. Left: Unstable ABI—new torch requires vLLM to rebuild. Right: Stable ABI—vLLM can import new torch directly. Note: Compatibility between vLLM and PyTorch still depends on other factors, including Python APIs, GPU-related requirements (such as the minimum supported CUDA version), and third-party dependencies. The LibTorch Stable ABI addresses binary compatibility but does not eliminate these other constraints. An application binary interface (ABI) defines how compiled code interacts with a library: how functions are called, data is laid out, and symbols are named. Even if an API looks the same in source code, an ABI change can force extensions to rebuild. A stable ABI preserves a supported set of binary interfaces across compatible versions, so extensions that use them can keep working without a rebuild. PyTorch's LibTorch Stable ABI has three layers: a stable C shim exposing selected LibTorch APIs, C++ wrappers that make the shim easier to use, and headeronly utilities in torch::headeronly that do not link against libtorch.so . Before the Stable ABI, a new PyTorch release could require a vLLM rebuild, delaying support for the new version and its features. With the Stable ABI, the same vLLM wheel can work across compatible PyTorch releases, letting users upgrade sooner and reducing rebuilds for package distributors. For developers, this means you can update and rebuild PyTorch, then test those changes in vLLM without rebuilding vLLM. Left: vLLM needs to change as LibTorch changes. Right: vLLM can change independent of LibTorch. The LibTorch Stable ABI is a limited subset of all of LibTorch. While many common ops are already supported through the C shim and through the higher level C++ convenience wrappers, not all are. model:vllm|ver:3.1|variant:pro|title:vll.content_excerpt: Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. Each sparse attention layer has a small indexer next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our DeepSeek-V3.2 post covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. Figure 1: Sparse attention (DSA) in Kimi K3.1 Pro. The indexer scores every past token, keeps the top 2,048, and every query head attends exactly over only those tokens' latents. Step through it. The index keys are a second per-token cache next to the MLA latent. Under tensor parallelism (TP) both are replicated on every GPU; KDA state is per request, as in K3. The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8. Figure 2: Measured KV cache capacity on 8× GB300. Change the latent and index-key formats, the parallelism, or the context length to see how many full contexts fit. Each DSA layer stores two per-token caches of different widths: the MLA latent (576 bytes in FP8, 352 in NVFP4) and the index keys (132 bytes in FP8, 68 in MXFP4). story|title:agents are going async.content_excerpt: Imagine a chief of staff who disappears every time you hand them a big project and only comes back once it's done. You'd probably fire them immediately. A good chief of staff keeps projects moving in the background while staying reachable and keeping you updated along the way. As we ask agents to work toward bigger goals, they need the same two properties. An agent has to be responsive, acting on a new instruction right away with the context of everything before it, and productive, making progress on many large tasks at once. The architecture we've used to build agents for a while can't meet both requirements. In a standard ReAct loop, each long tool call blocks the loop and every other task queues behind it. Instead, we're seeing the ecosystem converge on a split between one agent that stays with the user and background workers that do the long work. Claude Code runs subagents in the background by default, OpenAI's dots hand work to background workers to make progress on several things at once, and DeepSeek Harness built its super agent around a router that talks to people and background workers that run tasks in parallel. We’re bringing this pattern to Deep Agents with async subagents . An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop. An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later. Steering a running subagent is separate from reaching the orchestrator. When the orchestrator sends a follow-up with update_async_task , the update_strategy field on that subagent's definition decides what happens: Every unfinished task is listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what's in flight. It can poll with check_async_task or tasks can report back on their own : A subagent that needs approval shows up as waiting , and the user answers on the subagent's own thread without interrupting the orchestrator. story|title:dharma field extractor any d.content_excerpt: A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost. In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE , a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task. OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing. However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record. Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database. A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem. So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. story|title:gdpx measuring frontier mode.content_excerpt: GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities. We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI , not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead. We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available. We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin . Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is also the best model for materials science. Our finance and legal tasks are so challenging that basically every model scores exactly 0. Interestingly, if you subset to a single model family, you will sometimes see very similar spikes. The cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely. It’s impossible to make all the nuanced comparisons enabled by GDPx in a single newsletter. story|title:how we optimized browser use.content_excerpt: Browser agents can now take on multi-step work that's painful and time-consuming for people. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse plan cross-country road trips, cancel unused subscriptions, and list cars for sale, all on sites with no public APIs. DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Browser use helps in two places: actions an API can't cover, like using a website the agent wasn't set up for, and end-to-end testing of the web apps coding agents build. Either way, the agent needs two things: This post focuses on the tools, and on making them good enough that the agent uses the browser well. We set out to give agents in Managed Deep Agents a browser. We compared seven toolsets and picked the best one, Stagehand ( GitHub ) from Browserbase . Then we improved it based on what agents did in LangSmith traces, and validated every change with evals. The biggest lesson was how much room there is to improve an agent through tool design. Browser use toolsets come in a few forms: native tools, an MCP server , or a CLI the agent runs in a shell. Browser use poses two unique challenges for those tools: We iterated with the agent development lifecycle : run the agent on a benchmark, read its traces in LangSmith to see where it wasted steps or tokens, change the tool, and run evals to check that the change helped. Every run was a LangSmith experiment , so we could compare setups side by side and click from any number into the trace behind it. We had every harness return structured output (a JSON answer). That way a formatting slip, like a one-line reply to a task that asks for a table, didn't count against its browsing. We upstreamed that option to Browserbase's evals. We first held the model and tasks fixed and changed only the toolset. The seven toolsets differ in how the agent calls them: Every toolset passed between 78% and 90% of tasks, but cost and speed varied widely. story|title:new context engineering chal.content_excerpt: It feels like everyone is converging on the same agent architecture: an LLM, running in a loop, calling tools, running in a sandbox. Claude Code - perhaps the first high profile manifestation of this - came out over a year and a half ago. Deep Agents , our agent harness, launched over a year ago. This pattern has been building for a while. There’s nothing bad with that convergence per se, but it has led to a sentiment among some AI engineers that I’ve talked to recently that “all the hard problems are solved” or “there’s no new AI engineering problems to solve”. When people express this sentiment, I think they are largely talking about the context engineering practices we do to make agents work. And to some extent they are right - there are a lot of standard-ish context engineering solutions we’ve all arrived at: The good news (for context engineering aficionados like myself) is that I think we’re seeing a step function change in agent capabilities, or at least how they are being used. Specifically, over the past few months every agent builder I’ve chatted with has been thinking about proactive, always on, goal-oriented agents . The core of this agent shares a lot of similarities with coding agents, but there are a set of new challenges as well. I highlight a few below. We (at LangChain, and in the industry) don’t necessarily have solutions (or at least, general solutions) for these, so thinking about these has been the most fun I’ve had in a while! How to be proactive without being annoying : These proactive agents run in the background and either listen to event feeds or are woken up with heartbeats. On one hand, they need to be able to push things to the user - that creates a sense of helping. On the other hand, if you push too many notifications to the user, you risk overwhelming them. story|title:the components of agent memo.content_excerpt: Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward , but it must be lived forward . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents. As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge. Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest , the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge. Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1). We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization. By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window). In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. story|title:uncensored llms in agent loo.content_excerpt: We gave every uncensored model tools and five multi-step tasks. Smarter originals finish more, models built on weaker ones loop almost twice as often, and most still fail half the time. Uncensored models are mostly sold on what they will say. We wanted to know what they do: give them tools and a multi-step job, and see whether they finish, go in circles, or fall over. We ran all 31 ranked models on the Open Uncensored API through the same five agent tasks (edit a file, browse pages, multi-step math with a calculator, debug code until tests pass, analyse data), each capped at 14 turns. The intelligence of the model an uncensored edit came from does predict agent reliability: the correlation between the two is 0.56 across 31 models. Models built on originals scoring 60 or more finished 38% of tasks on average; the rest finished 27%. Neither number is good. Even the strong group fails more often than it succeeds. A loop is the model repeating the same tool call three times without progress. A crash is a malformed tool call, a made-up tool result, or giving up on tools mid-task. Models built on weaker originals loop almost twice as often. Crashes are common in both groups, so a strong original does not make a model safe to leave unattended. Several originals have more than one uncensored version on the API. Tasks finished out of 5: So far the versions of one original land within a task of each other. With one run per task that gap is noise, so we cannot yet say whether abliteration, heretic edits or fine tunes cost tool use differently. More trials will tell. These are early numbers: one run per task, five tasks per model, so a single task is 20 points and small differences are noise. Tool calls are written in a text format rather than native function calling, which is harder on some models than others. story|title:vindexllm windows vulkan gpu.content_excerpt: VindexLLM is a pure Delphi, GPU-powered LLM inference engine that uses Vulkan compute shaders to run GGUF models entirely on the GPU. It performs full transformer inference without relying on Python, CUDA, or other external runtimes, requiring only vulkan-1.dll, which is typically included with modern GPU drivers. VindexLLM is a GPU-accelerated LLM inference engine written entirely in Delphi, using Vulkan compute shaders for all heavy computation. It loads standard GGUF model files, runs the full transformer forward pass on the GPU, and produces text — no Python, no CUDA toolkit, no external runtimes. The only dependency is vulkan-1.dll , which already ships with every modern GPU driver. Feed it a prompt, get tokens back. Everything between — embedding lookup, 34 layers of attention and FFN, normalization, sampling — happens on the GPU via GLSL 450 compute shaders compiled to SPIR-V and embedded as Windows resources into the binary. Load a model, generate text, done. The chat example adds multi-turn conversation with SQLite-backed persistent memory and RAG retrieval across sessions. For the full implementations including status callbacks, cancel support, event hooks, error handling, and performance stats, see testbed\UTest.Demo.pas . Most LLM inference stacks depend on CUDA (NVIDIA-only, ~3GB toolkit install), Python environments, or large runtime libraries. VindexLLM takes a different approach: VindexLLM implements the standard dense transformer forward pass. For each token, the engine runs 34 layers of attention and FFN computation on the GPU, then samples the next token from the output logits. Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel using batched matmul shaders. Autoregressive generation runs one token at a time using matvec shaders. Both paths share the same KV cache, which uses TQ3 compression to reduce VRAM usage by ~9× compared to F32. Dense inference is working end-to-end. The engine loads a Gemma 3 4B GGUF, tokenizes a prompt with chat template formatting, runs the full forward pass on the GPU, and generates coherent text with configurable sampling. A complete interactive chat system with persistent memory and RAG is built on top of the inference engine. story|title:why agents are soon only goi.content_excerpt: For the past two years, building capable Agents meant designing tools, figuring out which actions help the model complete a task, deciding how granular each tool schema needs to be, or iterating on system instruction templates. This is changing. Agents are moving in the opposite direction by collapsing their entire tool catalog into one tool : exec . This is called Code Mode (or Programmatic Tool Calling). Instead of forcing the model to trigger tools one at a time across turns, the harness gives the model a single exec(code) tool. The model writes a short TypeScript or Python script that chains, combines, and awaits actions inside an isolated sandbox. To understand why agents are converging on a single exec tool, we should look at how tool calling evolved. Initially, we only gave agents a handful of tools because they couldn't reliably choose or filter across a large catalog. As models improved, we connected dozens of tools or MCP servers, but ran into context window limits. We solved that with tool search and progressive disclosure , letting agents look up tools on demand. Even with dynamic tool loading, we still had dozens of individual tools, and were still stuck with the limitation of standard tool calling: one action per turn. In standard tool calling, the model generates a structured object (typically JSON) that defines a single action (or at best a flat batch of independent calls, like reading three files), waits for the raw output to come back, adds it into the prompt history, reasons again, and decides what to do next. From my own experience, we made a big jump recently in how reliably models can combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass: Several shifts came together to enable this. Frontier models are trained heavily on code, and providers have started post-training models for Code Mode. At the same time, MCP servers now increasingly ship outputSchema alongside inputSchema , giving the model upfront knowledge of return types so it can chain Tool A into Tool B inside the same script before seeing runtime output. Code Mode collapses the tool catalog into a single tool on the model surface: exec(code) . Instead of passing 80 separate JSON Schema tool objects to the model API, the agent compiles those schemas into compact type declarations ( declare namespace tools { ... } ). story|title:why human insight is a strat.content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. story|variant:small|title:palette teachi.content_excerpt: Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Nobody makes a deck in one pass. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard. Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate. Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard.
